rationale: The available literature on autosomal recessive intellectual developmental disorder 84 (OMIM #620401, associated with biallelic SGSM3 pathogenic variants) comprises only a handful of families worldwide. While Birnbaum et al. (2024) noted that affected individuals from Ashkenazi Jewish families exhibited emotional and behavioral challenges alongside intellectual disability, and PanelApp records mention hypotonia and behavioral challenges, there is no quantitative evidence or published cohort systematically demonstrating that hyperactive behavior, restlessness, and stereotypic movements (HP:0000752, HP:0000733) occur in >60% of individuals. Furthermore, Turkyilmaz et al. (2025) identified two affected siblings with biallelic loss-of-function variants who presented with nonsyndromic intellectual disability and short stature without reported hyperactivity or stereotypic movements. Therefore, the specific threshold claim (>60% prevalence of hyperactivity, restlessness, and stereotypic movements) is not supported by documented patient counts in the peer-reviewed literature.

evidence.text: Birnbaum et al. characterized an intellectual disability syndrome segregating with a homozygous founder variant in SGSM3 in Ashkenazi Jewish families, noting moderate intellectual disability and emotional and behavioural challenges, but did not define a confirmed >60% incidence of specific stereotypic movements or hyperactivity across evaluated cohorts.

source.title: Intellectual disability syndrome associated with a homozygous founder variant in SGSM3 in Ashkenazi Jews
source.quote: We describe the clinical features … had moderate intellectual disability, emotional and behavioural challenges…

evidence.text: Turkyilmaz et al. identified a novel homozygous stop-gain variant (NM_015705.6: c.1576C>T: p.(Arg526Ter)) in SGSM3 in two Turkish siblings presenting with nonsyndromic intellectual disability and short stature, demonstrating that behavioral disturbances and stereotypic movements are not obligate features across all biallelic cases.

source.title: A Strong Candidate Gene for Nonsyndromic Intellectual Disability Phenotype: SGSM3
source.quote: In this study, a novel homozygous stop-gain (NM_015705.6: c.1576C>T: p.(Arg526Ter)) variation was detected in the SGSM3 gene in two siblings with short stature and ID findings. The report of two cases with bi-allelic LOF variants in the SGSM3 gene from different populations with similar clinical manifestations strengthens the potential of this gene as a candidate gene for the nonsyndromic ID phenotype.

new_directions.question_text: What is the systematic HPO-coded phenotype profile and exact frequency of behavioral abnormalities across all reported SGSM3 biallelic probands worldwide?
new_directions.rationale: Because fewer than 10 families are described in the literature, compiling standardized HPO terms across international cohorts is necessary to establish whether behavioral features are recurrent or represent ascertainment bias.

new_directions.question_text: Do loss-of-function variants in SGSM3 result in altered dopaminergic or Ras/MAPK signaling predisposing to hyperactivity or stereotypies in cellular or animal models?
new_directions.rationale: SGSM proteins modulate Ras/Rap signaling in fetal and adult brain; functional neurodevelopmental models can test whether SGSM3 loss directly drives hyperactive or stereotypic behavior.
